raw.answer: The case asked what legal effect follows when an adoption breaks the Civil Code rule that the adopter must be at least 20 years older than the adopted child. The court decided that such an adoption is not automatically void. It can only be undone if someone asks a court to annul it.
raw.held: An adoption that violates the Civil Code Article 1073 age rule (adopter at least 20 years older than the adoptee) can only be annulled by a court on request and is not void automatically. The earlier interpretation Yuan-Jie No. 3120, item 5, is maintained.

points.text: The earlier interpretation reasoned that marriage and adoption both create status relationships, so the rules for annulling an unlawful marriage should apply by analogy to an unlawful adoption, since the Civil Code has no separate annulment rule for adoption.

The Code of Civil Procedure, enacted after the Civil Code, sets special procedures for lawsuits to annul an adoption, which presumes that the Civil Code recognizes such annulment. The court found the earlier reading not improper.
The earlier interpretation has stood for a long time. Changing it suddenly could cause many people who already hold adoptive status to face family and social disputes and great harm.
The claim that an adopter had an unlawful profit motive falls under Civil Code Article 72, a separate matter. It does not affect the age-limit interpretation and cannot justify changing it.

who: People adopted in violation of the age rule
Adopters who broke the age gap rule
Families and others relying on existing adoptions

raw.answer: The case asked whether the National Assembly, the Legislative Yuan and the Control Yuan count as a democratic country's parliament. The court decided that, taken together, these three bodies are equivalent to the parliament of a democratic country.
raw.held: The National Assembly, the Legislative Yuan and the Control Yuan together are to be regarded as equivalent to the parliament of a democratic country.

points.text: The Constitution was based on Sun Yat-sen's teachings and set up five Yuan alongside the National Assembly, so it cannot easily be compared with a separation of three powers.

The National Assembly exercises political power for the nation's citizens, the Legislative Yuan is the highest legislative body, and the Control Yuan is the highest supervisory body. Each is made up of representatives or members chosen directly or indirectly by the people.
The powers they exercise are important powers of a democratic country's parliament.

Some methods differ from other democracies' parliaments, such as meeting regularly each year, majority quorum and majority decisions. But in constitutional position and the nature of their powers, the three bodies together are equivalent to a parliament.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who does military service by taking another person's name counts as having military status. The court said no: serving under someone else's name is unlawful, so the person is hard to regard as having military status. The court also kept in place its earlier Interpretation Yuan-Zi No. 2684.
raw.held: Doing military service under another person's name is an illegal act, so the person cannot easily be regarded as having military status. Interpretation Yuan-Zi No. 2684 remains upheld.

points.text: Serving in the military under another person's name is an unlawful act.
Because the act is unlawful, the person is hard to recognize as having military status.
The court's earlier Interpretation Yuan-Zi No. 2684 should still be maintained.

who: People who served in the military under another person's name

raw.answer: The case asked whether supplementary budgets (追加預算) count toward the total budget when applying the Constitution's minimum share for education, science and culture spending in cities and counties. The court decided they do not count. The 35 percent figure is measured against the total budget as drawn up at the start.
raw.held: The 35 percent minimum in Article 164 of the Constitution refers to the share of total annual expenditure when the budget is drawn up. Supplementary budgets are not included in that total.

points.text: The question was whether a supplementary budget is part of the total budget for the education, science and culture minimum.
Article 164 sets the minimum at 35 percent of the total budget in cities and counties, and this refers to the share of total expenditure at the time the budget is compiled.
A supplementary budget can only be proposed when budget execution runs into a situation listed in Article 53 of the Budget Act, so it arises later and is separate from the original budget.
For that reason, supplementary budgets are not included in the total budget used for the 35 percent calculation.

raw.answer: The case asked when a case involving the offences listed in Article 61 of the Criminal Code can be appealed to the third-instance court. The court said that such cases decided by the second instance generally cannot be appealed to the third instance. If a third-instance court does not dismiss such an appeal, it does not follow the required legal procedure.
raw.held: Cases for offences listed in Article 61 that were decided at the second instance cannot be appealed to the third instance, unless a party argued before the end of oral argument that the offence is not one listed there and the second instance still treated it as one. Where the prosecutor did not dispute the law applied and the case has no link to appealable cases, the third-instance court should dismiss the appeal.

points.text: A final judgment of the Supreme Court binds the parties; any error can only be remedied through the legally set routes. The question here was still answered because whether an appeal to the third instance is allowed is a threshold procedural issue on which views differed.

Under Article 368 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 61 offences decided in the second instance cannot be appealed to the third-instance court. This applies where the prosecutor did not dispute the law applied and the case has no link to appealable cases.
If the third-instance court does not dismiss such an appeal under Article 387 of the same Code, that does not meet the required legal form.

If it is disputed whether a case is an Article 61 offence, it depends on whether a party raised this before the end of oral argument in the second instance. Only if a party had claimed it was not an Article 61 offence, and the second instance still ruled it was, may an appeal go to the third instance.

raw.answer: The case asked who counts as a "judicial official" (司法人員) under Article 37 of the Lawyers Act. The court said the term includes court clerks (書記官) who are appointed under the Court Organization Act and handle judicial matters. It does not include clerks sent to courts by accounting agencies to handle accounting work.
raw.held: The judicial officials in Article 37 of the Lawyers Act include clerks appointed under the Court Organization Act who handle judicial affairs, but not accounting clerks posted to courts by accounting agencies.

points.text: The Enforcement Rules of the Lawyers Act (Article 12) do list court clerks among judicial officials.
That listing refers only to clerks appointed under the Court Organization Act who handle judicial matters.
Clerks posted to courts by accounting agencies to handle accounting affairs are therefore not included.

who: Court clerks appointed under the Court Organization Act
Accounting clerks posted to courts by accounting agencies
Lawyers subject to Article 37 of the Lawyers Act

raw.answer: The case asked under what conditions a farmland lease can be ended because the tenant gave up farming it on their own. The court decided that a lease still within its term can only be ended in the situations listed in Article 17 of the Farmland 37.5% Rent Reduction Act. If a tenant gives up farming, there must also be a proper reason of moving away or changing occupation.
raw.held: A farmland lease that has not reached the end of its term cannot be ended unless one of the situations listed in Article 17 of the Farmland 37.5% Rent Reduction Act applies. When a tenant gives up the right to farm, under item 2 of that article there must truly be a proper reason, namely moving away or changing occupation.

points.text: Before the lease period ends, a farmland lease may be ended only in the situations listed in Article 17 of the Farmland 37.5% Rent Reduction Act.
A tenant's voluntary giving up of farming falls under item 2 of that article, which also requires a real, proper reason of moving away or changing occupation.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant who was sentenced to loss of public rights, but whose main sentence was suspended (probation), may serve as a public servant during the probation period. The court said yes, unless some other disqualifying restriction applies. The quoted paragraphs do not set out the court's reasons.
raw.held: A public servant sentenced to loss of public rights whose main sentence is suspended may, during the probation period, serve as a public servant, unless other disqualifying restrictions apply.

points.text: The question was whether a public servant given a suspended sentence could hold public office during probation.
The court held that during probation such a person is not barred from serving, unless another disqualification applies.

who: People sentenced to loss of public rights

raw.answer: The case asked whether an adopted child may marry a biological child of the adoptive parents before the adoption has been ended. The court said that if the adoptive parent has died, the adopted child can no longer end the adoption, so the marriage is not allowed. There is an exception where, at the time of adoption, the adoptive parent truly meant for the adopted child to marry their biological child.
raw.held: After an adoptive parent dies, an adopted child who can no longer end the adoption may not marry the adoptive parents' biological child. The exception is where the adoptive parent genuinely intended the marriage at the time of adoption.

points.text: An adopted child who wants to marry the adoptive parents' biological child must first end the adoption, as an earlier interpretation (No. 32) already provides.

If the adoptive parent has died and did not, while alive, arrange the marriage (as in interpretation No. 58), the adopted child has no way to end the adoption, so the marriage is not legally permitted.
This restriction applies only to adoptions that are real adoptions under the civil law.

Where the adoptive parent truly intended at the time that the child would marry their biological child, such as with arrangements like taking in a girl for a boy or a boy for a girl, it is not a civil-law adoption, so the restriction does not apply.

raw.answer: The case asked what it means to "continue to take part in" a rebel organization. The court decided that anyone who once joined such an organization is treated as still taking part until they turn themselves in or other facts show they have really left. A note says that, under Interpretation No. 556, parts of this ruling that do not match that later interpretation are to be changed.
raw.held: Anyone who once joined a rebel organization is treated as continuing to take part until they turn themselves in or other facts prove they left. If this continued after the Act for Punishment of Rebellion took effect on June 21, 1949, Article 2 of the Criminal Code does not apply, and the amnesty and sentence-reduction order cannot be used for conduct continuing after December 31, 1946.

points.text: A person who once joined a rebel organization is regarded as continuing to take part unless they turned themselves in or other facts show they truly left.

If the person was still in this continuing state after the Act for Punishment of Rebellion took effect on June 21, 1949, the change in law did not come after the act, so Article 2 of the Criminal Code does not apply.
The amnesty and sentence-reduction order only covered offenses up to December 31, 1946, so it cannot be used if the offense was still continuing after that date.
A note says that under Interpretation No. 556, parts of this ruling inconsistent with that interpretation are to be changed.

who: People who joined a rebel organization
People whose participation continued after June 21, 1949
People seeking the amnesty or sentence-reduction order

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the 1959 short-term government bond regulation saying the bonds "may not be reported lost" meant that holders of lost bonds could not use the court's public notice procedure under the Civil Code. The court decided it did not. The regulation's wording does not remove the Civil Code procedure.
raw.held: The public notice procedure in Article 725 of the Civil Code protects lawful holders of bearer securities. Article 3 of the 1959 short-term bond regulation, which only says "may not be reported lost," cannot be used to exclude that Civil Code article.

points.text: The Civil Code's public notice procedure exists to protect the interests of lawful holders of bearer securities.
"May not be reported lost" only means a holder cannot ask the issuer to stop payment on a lost bond, so the issuer has no duty to do so.

Public notice is a different thing: the last holder of a lost bearer security asks a court to call on rights-holders to come forward, and after a judgment extinguishing the lost certificate's effect, the holder can assert the rights against the issuer.
Because the regulation does not expressly exclude Article 725 of the Civil Code, the "may not be reported lost" wording alone cannot show that holders may not apply for public notice.

who: Last holders of lost bearer securities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a prosecutor must formally decide not to prosecute the person who was falsely accused when the person who filed the complaint turns out to have lied. The court said the prosecutor may go straight to prosecuting the false accuser without separately issuing a non-prosecution decision for the accused person. However, if the original complainant applies for it, the prosecutor must still issue that decision afterward.
raw.held: A prosecutor who finds the complainant made a false accusation may prosecute that false accusation directly, without separately issuing a non-prosecution decision for the falsely accused person. But if the original complainant makes a request about the original complaint, the prosecutor must still issue a non-prosecution decision in writing afterward.

points.text: The question was whether a prosecutor must issue a non-prosecution decision for the falsely accused person when the complainant is found to have made a false accusation.
The prosecutor may prosecute the false accusation directly, with no need to separately issue a non-prosecution decision for the accused person.
If the original complainant makes a request about the original complaint, the prosecutor must still add a written non-prosecution decision.

who: Original complainants found to have made false accusations

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the Control Yuan (a supervisory member) may also serve as a director, supervisor or manager of a privately owned company. The court decided that the work these company roles involve counts as the 'carrying on of business' that Article 103 of the Constitution bars Control Yuan members from doing.
raw.held: The business carried out by directors, supervisors and managers of privately owned companies falls within the 'carrying on of business' that Article 103 of the Constitution refers to.

points.text: Article 103 bars Control Yuan members from holding other public office and from carrying on business.
The business restriction exists to let the supervisory power be exercised properly and to keep members in an impartial position above the fray.
Directors, supervisors and managers of private companies all carry out the company's business.
That business does not fit with exercising a Control Yuan member's powers, so it falls within what Article 103 forbids.

raw.answer: The case asked which court should hear disputes that arise when public farmland given out to people under Taiwan's farmland allotment measures is cancelled or rescinded. The court decided that ordinary (civil) courts have jurisdiction over these disputes. It reasoned that the allotment is a private-law sale contract, not a compulsory government act.
raw.held: When an administrative office allots public farmland to people under the Taiwan Province measures for allotting public farmland to support owner-farmers, disputes arising from cancelling or rescinding the allotment are to be heard by the ordinary courts.

points.text: The measures were meant to support owner-farmers by allotting public farmland to those who work it, and taking up an allotment is voluntary, not compulsory.
The allotment is the government acting for the state to make a private-law sale contract with the person receiving the land.
Under Article 14, item 4 of the measures, the contract is formed once the allotment certificate is issued.
So disputes over cancelling or rescinding that contract should be resolved through civil litigation.
Disputes over land taken back under the Land-to-the-Tiller Act have long gone to the administrative court, which the highest courts do not contest, so the ruling does not address them.

who: People who received allotted public farmland
Administrative offices that allot public farmland

raw.answer: The case asked whether certain children in adoptive families can inherit in place of a family member who died before the inheritance opened (substitute inheritance). The court decided that the biological children of an adopted child, the adopted children of an adopted child, and the adopted children of a biological child can all inherit this way.
raw.held: The court held that the biological children of adopted children, the adopted children of adopted children, and the adopted children of biological children all have the right of substitute inheritance.

points.text: The court noted that the relationship between an adopted child and adoptive parents is a legal (fictional) blood relationship, as Interpretation No. 28 already explained.
When an heir dies before the inheritance begins, that is a different situation from Interpretation No. 57, which dealt with an heir who renounces the inheritance.
On that basis, the three kinds of descendants named in the question may inherit in place of the deceased heir.
The phrase 'unless the law provides otherwise' in Article 1077 of the Civil Code refers to cases where the law makes an exception for legal blood relatives, such as Article 1142, paragraph 2.

who: Adopted children of adopted or biological children

raw.answer: The case asked whether the act of bribing a public official, described in Article 122, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code, counts as a crime of malfeasance in office. The court decided it does not. Bribery is an independent offense, and the same goes for helping or inciting it.
raw.held: The bribe-giving act in Article 122, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code is not, by its nature, a crime of malfeasance in office, and the same applies to people who help or incite it.

points.text: Malfeasance crimes require the offender to hold a particular status, but the bribe-giving act in Article 122, paragraph 3 does not require any special status.

Its elements of the offense and its rules on reducing or waiving punishment differ from those for a public official taking bribes, so it is an independent crime and Article 31, paragraph 1 does not apply.
Helping or inciting bribe-giving falls under Articles 29 and 30, with no room for Article 31, paragraph 1.

Offering or handing over a bribe is a crime whether or not the other side agrees or accepts, while an agreement to a bribe demand does not necessarily amount to a crime. The two acts therefore differ in nature, are not necessarily joint offenses, and the general complicity rules do not apply.
Article 122 lists bribe-giving alongside bribe-taking only for legislative convenience, as Article 132, paragraph 3 does with non-officials who leak non-defense secrets.

who: People who help or incite bribe-giving

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who served three or more years in a recommended-rank (薦任) auditing post can apply to take the accountant qualification examination by review (檢覈). The court decided that people who held such a post in a government agency for at least three years and passed the official rank-qualification process are treated as meeting the accountant law's requirement. The ruling as provided does not give the court's reasoning.
raw.held: Anyone who held a recommended-rank auditing post in a government agency for three or more years and was qualified through the official rank-certification process is to be treated as meeting Article 2, paragraph 1, item 4 of the Accountant Act.

points.text: The question was whether three or more years in a recommended-rank auditing post lets someone apply for the accountant qualification review.
The court said such service, with qualification through the rank-certification process, counts as meeting Article 2, paragraph 1, item 4 of the Accountant Act.

who: People who served three or more years in recommended-rank auditing posts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a company officer who is not in the business of giving guarantees can bind the company by guaranteeing someone else's debt in the company's name. The court said no: under Article 23 of the Company Law, such a company generally cannot act as a guarantor, so an officer's guarantee in the company's name does not take effect against the company.
raw.held: A company that is not allowed to act as a guarantor under Article 23 of the Company Law is not bound when its officer guarantees someone in the company's name. That act is not treated as the company's act and has no effect on the company.

points.text: Article 23 of the Company Law says a company may not be a guarantor for anyone, unless another law or its articles of incorporation make guarantees part of its business.
If an officer breaks this rule and gives a guarantee in the company's name, it cannot be regarded as the company's own act.
Because it is not the company's act, it has no effect on the company.

who: Companies not in the guarantee business

raw.answer: The case asked whether a particular kind of light rail track (輕便軌道) counts as immovable property (real estate). The court decided that such tracks are real estate, unless they were laid only temporarily. A track that stays attached to the land and serves a set economic purpose counts as real estate.
raw.held: Light rail tracks are to be treated as real estate, except those laid only temporarily. Tracks that stay attached to land and serve a set economic purpose count as real estate.

points.text: The court relied on Article 66, paragraph 1 of the Civil Code, which refers to things fixed to land: not part of the land itself, continuously attached to it, serving a set economic purpose, and not easily moved.
A track laid on a continuing basis, as opposed to a temporary one, fits that description.
Even if such a track is rebuilt or altered, like a house it does not lose its character as a thing fixed to land, so it is treated as real estate.

raw.answer: The case asked whether courts below the High Court level should belong to the Judicial Yuan. The ruling says they should, because those courts handle civil and criminal trials, which the Constitution gives to the Judicial Yuan as the nation's highest judicial body. It also says the related laws and regulations need to be amended.
raw.held: Article 77 of the Constitution makes the Judicial Yuan the highest judicial body in charge of civil and criminal trials, which means trials in courts at every level. So the High Courts, the courts below them and their branch courts must belong to the Judicial Yuan.

points.text: Article 77 gives the Judicial Yuan, as the highest judicial body, charge of civil and criminal trials, and this means trials in courts at every level.

Article 82 provides that the organization of the Judicial Yuan and of the courts at each level is set by law, and it places this in the judicial chapter. This shows an aim of a single, consistent judicial system.
Since High Courts and lower courts and their branches hold civil and criminal trials, they must belong to the Judicial Yuan.
The related laws and regulations must be amended one by one to match the purpose of Article 77.

who: High Courts and lower courts and their branch courts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a National Assembly delegate may also serve as a provincial or county councillor. The court decided that they may not hold both positions at once, because the two offices have different roles and powers under the Constitution.
raw.held: A National Assembly delegate may not also serve as a member of a provincial or county council.

points.text: National Assembly delegates are elected in legally set electoral units, convene according to law, and exercise political power on behalf of the whole nation's citizens.
Provincial and county council members convene according to law and exercise the legislative power belonging to their own province or county.
The Constitution sets up different levels of representative bodies and gives them different powers, and holding both posts would undermine that purpose, so delegates cannot also be councillors.

raw.answer: The case was about how a court should hold and pay interest on money, securities or valuables that people deposit with it under the deposit law. The court decided that where the court's location has a bank that acts as the state treasury agent, the items go to that bank's treasury department, and interest is paid under Article 8 of the deposit law.
raw.held: Where a local court's location has a bank acting as state treasury agent, the court must hand deposited money, securities and valuables to that bank's treasury department for safekeeping, and interest must be paid as Article 8 of the deposit law requires.

points.text: Article 4, paragraph 2 of the deposit law specially provides for safekeeping by the treasury-agent bank, aiming to protect the interests of the parties concerned.
Keeping deposits in the bank's treasury department protects those interests better than keeping them in the bank's business department.

Article 8 of the deposit law clearly requires interest on deposited money, and the Ministry of Finance replied that treasury-held deposits can earn interest, which fits Article 8, so the treasury department is the proper place.

who: People who make deposits with courts
Parties with an interest in deposited items

raw.answer: The Executive Yuan and the National Assembly Secretariat asked how to count the 'total number' of National Assembly delegates, because delegates could not be re-elected and many vacancies could not be filled. The court decided that, for now, the total means the number of lawfully elected delegates who are able to answer the call and attend a meeting.
raw.held: Under present conditions, the constitution's 'total number of National Assembly delegates' is counted as the lawfully elected delegates who can respond to the summons and assemble.

points.text: The question arose because delegates could not be re-elected, many vacancies had no one to fill them, and the Assembly's third session was about to meet and needed a total to calculate attendance.
In the first and second sessions the total was the number of delegates who were supposed to be lawfully elected, but circumstances have since changed greatly.
After the major upheaval in the country more than ten years earlier, some delegates lost their freedom and could not attend, and many vacancies could not be filled.

Bodies set up by the constitution are meant to be able to exercise their powers, and the framers did not foresee the Assembly being unable to perform its constitutional function because of these obstacles.

To respect the purpose of establishing the National Assembly, the total is the lawfully elected delegates able to answer the call and meet where the central government is located; those able to attend but who do not are still included.

raw.answer: The case asked what the phrase "local public body" (地方公共團體) means in Article 3, item 2 of the Temple Supervision Act (監督寺廟條例). The court decided that it means a group that handles public affairs within a certain area, under laws or established custom. The paragraphs given do not set out the court's reasons or the facts of the underlying dispute.
raw.held: The phrase "local public body" in Article 3, item 2 of the Temple Supervision Act means a group that, under laws or custom, handles public affairs within a certain area.

points.text: The question was what "local public body" means in Article 3, item 2 of the Temple Supervision Act.
The court defined it as a group that handles public affairs within a certain area, whether by law or by custom.

who: Temples covered by the Temple Supervision Act
Groups that handle public affairs in a particular area

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant who was convicted of corruption but given a suspended sentence (probation) may take civil service exams or hold public office before the probation period ends. The court decided that such a person must wait until the probation period is over without the suspension being revoked. Only then may they take any exam or be appointed as a public servant.
raw.held: A person who had public service and was finally convicted of corruption, even with a suspended sentence, may take any exam or be appointed a public servant only after the probation period ends and the suspension has not been revoked.

points.text: The situations listed in Article 8, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Examination Act and Article 17, item 2 of the Civil Service Appointment Act count as the 'other negative qualifications' described in Interpretation No. 56.
A person who served in public office and was finally convicted of corruption is covered by these disqualifications, even if given a suspended sentence.
So the suspended sentence does not lift the bar right away; it ends only when probation expires without revocation.

who: Former public servants convicted of corruption
People given suspended sentences for corruption
Candidates for appointment as public servants

raw.answer: The case asked under what conditions a public servant may take on temporary work for a foreign organization. The court said that earlier rulings (Nos. 6 and 11) were based on the limits in Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Civil Servants Service Act. It held that if off-hours temporary work for a foreign organization interferes with the nature or dignity of the person's official post, it is not allowed, whether or not it is ordinarily called a business.
raw.held: A public servant who takes temporary work with a foreign organization in spare time is barred by the spirit of Article 14(1) of the Civil Servants Service Act if the work interferes with the nature or dignity of their official post, whether or not it is customarily called a business.

points.text: Interpretations No. 6 and No. 11 were made under the limits in Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Civil Servants Service Act.
The test is whether the temporary work with a foreign organization interferes with the nature or dignity of the official post.
Whether the work is ordinarily or customarily called a business does not matter; interfering work falls outside what the spirit of that article permits.

who: Foreign organizations that hire temporary workers

raw.answer: The case asked whether a soldier who has been absent from camp without permission for over a month, and who then commits another offense, is still tried by a military court. The court said such a soldier has already lost active-duty military status under the Military Service Act, so the offense is handled as it would be for a non-military person. The court also changed its earlier Interpretation Yuan-Tze No. 2822.
raw.held: A soldier absent without approval for more than one month has lost active-duty status under Article 20, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the Military Service Act. If he commits another offense, the trial court is decided as for a non-military person, and Yuan-Tze No. 2822 is changed.

points.text: Under Article 20, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the Military Service Act, a soldier absent without approval for over a month has lost active-duty military status.
Because he is no longer active-duty military, the court that tries any other offense he commits is decided as for a non-military person.
As a result, the earlier Yuan-Tze No. 2822 interpretation is changed.

who: Soldiers absent without leave for over one month
Soldiers who commit another offense while absent

raw.answer: The case asked whether a soldier who deserts while wearing only his own identification symbol can be punished under the ordinary desertion offense. The court held that wearing only that symbol is not comparable to taking other important items under Article 95 of the Army, Navy and Air Force Criminal Law, so it is ordinary desertion. The court also changed an earlier interpretation on this point.
raw.held: A soldier who deserts carrying only his own identification symbol is not treated as taking other important items under Article 95 of the Army, Navy and Air Force Criminal Law, and is punished for ordinary desertion. The earlier interpretation, Yuan-zi No. 2044, is changed on this part.

points.text: Carrying only one's own identification symbol is hard to regard as equivalent to the 'other important items' that Article 95 of the Army, Navy and Air Force Criminal Law refers to.
So such a soldier should be punished for ordinary desertion.
The earlier interpretation, Yuan-zi No. 2044, is changed on this part.

who: Military personnel carrying only their own identification symbol

raw.answer: The case asked whether a civil servant who has been stripped of civil rights (公權) can serve as a lawyer. The court decided that when a civil servant is sentenced to loss of civil rights for an act, the separate disciplinary penalty of dismissal is absorbed into that sentence, so Article 2, item 4 of the Lawyers Act can still apply to that person. The court also said its earlier Interpretation No. 2658 should be supplemented accordingly.
raw.held: When a civil servant is sentenced to loss of civil rights for the same act, the disciplinary penalty of dismissal is absorbed by that sentence, and Article 2, item 4 of the Lawyers Act is not excluded from applying. Interpretation No. 2658 is to be supplemented.

points.text: Under Article 36, item 1 of the Criminal Code, loss of civil rights removes the qualification to be a civil servant, and its effect is heavier than the disciplinary penalty of dismissal.

So when a civil servant is sentenced to loss of civil rights for the same act, the dismissal penalty is absorbed by it and no further disciplinary procedure is needed, as Article 25 of the Civil Servants Discipline Act makes clear.
Because of this, it is hard to rule out the application of Article 2, item 4 of the Lawyers Act, so Interpretation No. 2658 needs to be supplemented.

who: Civil servants sentenced to loss of civil rights
People who want to become lawyers

raw.answer: The case asked how someone who forges or alters New Taiwan Dollar notes should be punished. The court decided that the Act for Punishing Harm to the National Currency covers only national currency notes, and that New Taiwan Dollars are local notes, so forging or altering them is handled under the Criminal Code.
raw.held: The forged or altered notes in Article 3 of the Act mean national currency notes only. Because New Taiwan Dollars are local notes, forging or altering them is punished under the Criminal Code.

points.text: The question was how forging or altering New Taiwan Dollars should be punished.
Article 3 of the Act for Punishing Harm to the National Currency, which speaks of forged or altered notes, refers only to national currency notes.
New Taiwan Dollars are local notes, so forgery or alteration of them falls under the Criminal Code.

who: People accused of forging or altering New Taiwan Dollars

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Estate Tax Act applies to cases that arose before the Act was promulgated. The court decided that, because the Act has no explicit provision giving it retroactive effect, the proviso to Article 8 does not apply to cases where the inheritance began before the Act was promulgated.
raw.held: The Estate Tax Act has no express retroactive provision, so the proviso to its Article 8 does not apply to inheritances that began before the Act was promulgated.

points.text: The issue was whether the Estate Tax Act has retroactive effect for cases before its promulgation.
The current Estate Tax Act contains no explicit provision for retroactive effect.
Therefore the Article 8 proviso does not apply to cases where the inheritance began before the Act was promulgated.

who: People whose inheritance began before the Estate Tax Act was promulgated
Heirs affected by the Article 8 proviso

raw.answer: The case asked whether directors and supervisors who represent private shareholders in state-run enterprises are covered by the Civil Servants Service Act. The court decided that they are covered. It reasoned that they are service personnel of the state-run enterprise, and the Act applies to all such personnel.
raw.held: Directors and supervisors of public enterprises who represent private shareholders are subject to the Civil Servants Service Act.

points.text: Article 24 of the Civil Servants Service Act expressly says that all service personnel of public enterprises are covered by the Act.

Directors and supervisors representing private shares are service personnel of the public enterprise, so they cannot be excluded from the Act; the court points to earlier Interpretations No. 24 and No. 27.
The earlier Yuan Interpretation No. 3486 was issued before the State-Owned Enterprise Management Act was promulgated, so it does not apply to enterprises where government capital exceeds 50 percent.

who: Directors of public enterprises representing private shareholders
Supervisors of public enterprises representing private shareholders

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public official who holds a second post under a law or regulation may receive the public expense allowance attached to that second post. The court said yes where the official's main post has no such allowance but the second post does. The official still may not collect a second salary or a second allowance where the main post already provides one.
raw.held: Under Article 14, paragraph 2 of the Civil Servant Service Act, an official holding a concurrent post under law may receive only the salary and allowance of the main post. If the main post has no public expense allowance but the concurrent post does, the official may receive the concurrent post's allowance.

points.text: The question was whether an official serving in a concurrent post under law or regulation may receive that post's public expense allowance.
The rule against receiving a second salary or a second allowance for a concurrent post is read to mean the official can draw only the main post's salary and allowance.
Because of that reading, an official whose main post has no allowance but whose concurrent post has one may receive the concurrent post's allowance.

who: Public officials holding concurrent posts under law
Public officials whose main post has no public expense allowance

raw.answer: The case asked whether an adoption can be ended by court order when both sides have in substance agreed to end it but the required formalities were not completed. The court held that in a specific situation, where an adoptive daughter was formally married to the adoptive parent's biological son and the parent then died, she may ask a court to end the adoption.
raw.held: Where an adopted daughter was formally married by her adoptive parent to the parent's biological son, the substantive requirement for ending the adoption is met. If the adoptive parent died before the written formality could be completed, she may ask a court for a ruling ending the adoption under Article 1081, item 6 of the Civil Code.

points.text: Article 1080 requires both sides to agree to end an adoption and to put it in writing, and the writing requirement exists to make the act solemn.

When the adoptive parent presides over the daughter's formal marriage to the parent's biological son, both sides have agreed to change their status, which meets the substantive requirement in the first paragraph of Article 1080.
If the adoptive parent dies before completing the written formality, completing it becomes impossible.
So the daughter may seek a court ruling ending the adoption under Article 1081, item 6, as a remedy.

who: Adopted daughters who were formally married to the adoptive parent's biological son
Adoptive parents who arranged such a marriage
Courts handling requests to end adoptions

raw.answer: The case asked how forging or altering New Taiwan Dollars should be punished. The court decided that, from the date the Central Bank entrusted the Bank of Taiwan with issuing them, forging or altering these notes is punished under the Act for Punishing Harm to National Currency.
raw.held: New Taiwan Dollars issued by the Bank of Taiwan, from the date the Central Bank entrusted it to issue them as agent, are covered by the Act for Punishing Harm to National Currency if forged or altered.

points.text: The New Taiwan Dollar was originally a local currency issued by the Bank of Taiwan.
After the Central Bank entrusted the Bank of Taiwan to issue it, the Central Bank handled printing and storage, paid the issuing costs, and held the related assets and liabilities.
Public and private accounting was also done in New Taiwan Dollars.

So from the entrusting date it should be seen as having the function of national currency under the Act, and forgery or alteration is punished under that Act to protect major national financial and economic interests during the period of mobilization against rebellion.
The ruling supplements the explanation given in Interpretation No. 63.

who: People who forge or alter New Taiwan Dollars

raw.answer: The case asked how to fix the date a law takes effect when the law says it applies from the day it is promulgated. The court decided that the relevant date is the one listed in the law's arrival-date table, not simply the promulgation day. The paragraphs provided give no further reasoning.
raw.held: The phrase in Article 1 of the Act on Law Enforcement Dates about the day a law is due to reach the competent offices means the date listed in the table of arrival dates. Laws that say they apply from promulgation still take effect from the date in that table, unless the law provides otherwise.

points.text: The question was how to set the effective date of a law that says it applies from its promulgation day.
The court read the 'day due to reach the competent offices' in Article 1 of the Act as the date listed in the law's arrival-date table.
So laws that apply from promulgation still take effect from the table date, unless the law provides otherwise.

who: Persons subject to laws that apply from promulgation

raw.answer: The case asked whether a pledgee (someone holding a pledged item as security) must first obtain an enforcement title before asking a court to auction the item. The court decided that when the pledgee auctions under the situation described in Article 893 of the Civil Code, the earlier Interpretation No. 980 still applies. If the pledgee does not auction it personally and instead asks a court to do so, an enforcement title must be obtained first.
raw.held: A pledgee who sells the pledged item in a situation covered by Civil Code Article 893 must still follow Interpretation No. 980. If they ask a court to auction it rather than doing so themselves, they must first obtain an enforcement title.

points.text: The question was whether a pledgee asking a court to auction the pledged item must first obtain an enforcement title.
Even in a situation under Civil Code Article 893, the pledgee must still follow Interpretation No. 980.
If the pledgee does not auction the item personally but applies to a court, an enforcement title must be obtained first.

who: Courts asked to auction pledged items

raw.answer: The case asked whether someone who has served at least three years in a recommended-rank (薦任) auditing post in the Ministry of National Defense may take the accountant qualification examination by review of credentials. The court said yes, in the situation it describes: the person must have held that post for three years or more and been reviewed and registered by the Ministry of Civil Service's appointment-ranking body (銓敘部). The ruling does not give detailed reasons beyond this.
raw.held: The phrase 'qualified through ranking' in Interpretation No. 67 means qualified through the Ministry of Civil Service (銓敘部). A person who has served three or more years in a recommended-rank auditing post in the Ministry of National Defense and has been reviewed and registered by that ministry is treated as meeting Article 2, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Accountant Act.

points.text: The court clarified that the phrase 'qualified through ranking' in Interpretation No. 67 refers to being found qualified by the Ministry of Civil Service.

A person with at least three years in a recommended-rank auditing post in the Ministry of National Defense, who has been reviewed and registered by the Ministry of Civil Service, is treated as meeting Article 2, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Accountant Act.

who: People who have served as recommended-rank auditors in the Ministry of National Defense for three years or more
Applicants for the accountant qualification review

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the National Assembly may also hold an office as a government official. The court decided that they are not barred from doing so, based on how the Constitution was drafted.
raw.held: National Assembly representatives are not prohibited from also serving as government officials.

points.text: The assembly that drafted the Constitution did not adopt proposals that representatives could not serve as officials, or that serving officials could not be elected as representatives.
Article 28, paragraph 3 of the Constitution only bars a serving official from being elected as a representative in the electoral district where the official's post is located.
From this, the court concluded that the drafters did not intend to bar representatives from also being officials.

raw.answer: The case asked what 'flagrant offender' (現行犯) means in the Constitution, who may arrest such a person, and whether a bribe taken for a breach-of-duty offense counts as 'stolen property' (贓物). The court held that the constitutional term covers both flagrant offenders and those treated as such under Article 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that anyone may arrest them on the spot, and that such bribes can count as stolen property.
raw.held: The constitutional 'flagrant offender' means those described in paragraph 2 of Article 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and those treated as such under paragraph 3. Anyone may arrest in the situations Article 88 covers, even if the offense was not unnoticed by investigators. A bribe taken for a breach-of-duty offense counts as 'stolen property' under Article 88(3)(2), including cash bribes that reasonably appear to be crime proceeds and whose holder is clearly suspect.

points.text: The Constitution's Article 8 leaves arrest of flagrant offenders to law, and Article 88 includes both actual flagrant offenders and those treated as such, so the constitutional term includes both; the Constitution cannot have two different meanings of the term.

Even when a case is under investigation and another offender is discovered, Article 88 situations allow anyone to arrest at once, because the article aims to prevent escape and destruction of evidence and sets no limit to offenses unnoticed by investigators.

A bribe taken for a breach-of-duty offense is not stolen property under the criminal law's receiving-stolen-goods offense, but it is obtained through crime, so it counts as stolen property under Article 88(3)(2).
Cash bribes are by nature replaceable items, so if they reasonably appear to be crime proceeds and the holder is clearly suspect, the same provision applies.

who: People who catch or arrest suspects in the act

raw.answer: The case asked whether it counts as 'substitute inheritance' (代位繼承) when an heir gives up their right to inherit. The court said it does not, because substitute inheritance only applies when an heir died, or lost the right to inherit, before the inheritance began. It added that if the adopted daughter and her married daughter both validly give up their inheritance, the married daughter's son may inherit.
raw.held: Giving up an inheritance does not raise a substitute inheritance issue, since that only covers heirs who died or lost inheritance rights before the inheritance began. If the adopted daughter and her married daughter validly renounce, the latter's son may inherit the estate of 'A'.

points.text: Under Civil Code Article 1140, substitute inheritance applies only where the heir died, or lost the right to inherit, before the inheritance began.
So the adopted daughter (乙) giving up her inheritance does not raise a substitute inheritance issue.
If 乙 and her married daughter validly give up their inheritance rights, the daughter's son is an heir of the same order under Article 1138, item 1.
Under the first part of Article 1176, paragraph 1, that son may therefore inherit 甲's estate.

who: Heirs who give up an inheritance

raw.answer: The case asked when a government notice of an administrative decision about a person becomes valid. The court decided that such a notice is an official document under the Official Document Format Act, so it must follow the format that law requires. Unless another law says otherwise, a notice that lacks the legal format is not a valid notice.
raw.held: A notice that an administrative agency makes to a person to communicate its decision is an official document, and unless another law provides otherwise, it is a lawful notice only if the document itself meets the legally required format.

points.text: A notice that sets out an administrative decision is made in the course of handling public business, so it is similar in nature to an official document under the Official Document Format Act.
Because of that, the format rules and limits for official documents plainly apply to it, unless another law says differently.
Where no other law provides otherwise, the document itself must have the legal format to be lawful; the court calls this the natural reading of Articles 1, 2(1)(5), 3, 4 and 6 of the Act.

raw.answer: The case asked how the Trademark Office should deliver documents when the person they are meant for is in an occupied (淪陷) area. The court decided that such documents cannot be delivered, so they may be announced in the official gazette instead.
raw.held: If the applicant or other person concerned is in an occupied area, documents the Trademark Office must deliver to them count as undeliverable. They may be publicly announced in the gazette under Article 30, paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law Enforcement Rules.

points.text: The question was how the Trademark Office should deliver documents to a recipient in an occupied area.
Documents for a recipient in an occupied area are treated as impossible to deliver.
Because of that, they may be announced in the gazette under Article 30, paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law Enforcement Rules.

who: Other persons concerned in occupied areas

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules that bar certain people from being civil servants also apply when the disqualifying situation arises after a person has already been appointed. The court decided that they do. It said that a person who is not allowed to be appointed for such a reason may be removed from the current post if the situation arises after appointment.
raw.held: The limit set out in Article 17, item 2 of the Civil Service Appointment Act also applies when the disqualifying situation arises after the person has been appointed.

points.text: Article 17 of the Civil Service Appointment Act lists disqualifications, which is different from the disciplinary grounds in the Civil Servants Discipline Act, which are limited to illegal conduct, neglect of duty, or other failures in duty.

Someone in the Article 17, item 2 situation may not be appointed as a civil servant, so if that situation arises after appointment, the legislative intent means the person may be removed from the current post.

For a civil servant who received a suspended sentence after a final judgment for corruption, the ruling refers to Interpretation No. 66: once the suspension period ends and the person is reappointed, the disciplinary penalty of demotion with pay reduction must still be carried out as the law provides.

who: Civil servants who later meet a disqualifying condition
Civil servants convicted of corruption with a suspended sentence

raw.answer: The question was whether a crime committed after a court judgment has become final is covered by the rules on combined punishment for multiple crimes. The court said it is not. A sentence for such a later crime is simply served together with the earlier sentence, even if the person committed the new crime during a probation (suspended sentence) period.
raw.held: A crime committed after a judgment has become final is outside the multiple-crimes combined punishment rules. Even if it was committed during probation, the new sentence is served together with the earlier one once the probation is revoked.

points.text: Under Article 50 of the Criminal Code, combined punishment for multiple crimes applies only to crimes committed before a judgment becomes final.
A crime committed after a final judgment has nothing to do with the combined punishment rules, so its sentence can only be served together with the earlier sentence.
If the person intentionally commits a crime during probation and is sentenced to imprisonment or more, the earlier probation is revoked and the sentences are served together.
In that case there is no need to set a combined sentence under Article 53 of the Criminal Code or Article 481 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

who: People who commit a new crime after a final judgment
People on probation who commit a new crime

raw.answer: The case asked whether the job protection given to career (permanent) prosecutors covers only those who are able to carry out their duties. The court said yes: the protection applies to prosecutors who can perform their work. A prosecutor who has been on sick leave beyond a certain period and in practice cannot work may be ordered to retire from the post, under a civil servant leave rule, until other rules are set.
raw.held: The protection for career prosecutors applies to those able to perform their duties. Until other rules are made in line with that protection, a prosecutor who has been on sick leave beyond a set period and in fact cannot work may be ordered to retire temporarily under Article 10 of the civil servant leave rules.

points.text: Career prosecutors are protected under Article 40, paragraph 2 of the Court Organization Act, except when transferred, as an earlier interpretation (No. 13) already confirmed.
That protection is meant for prosecutors who are able to perform their duties.

A prosecutor who has taken sick leave beyond a certain period and in fact cannot do the job falls outside that protection, so may be ordered to retire under Article 10 of the civil servant leave rules until other rules are set in line with the protection's spirit.

who: Prosecutors unable to work due to prolonged illness

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant who is sentenced to loss of civil rights (deprivation of public rights) in a final criminal judgment, but whose sentence is suspended (probation), has their job duties automatically suspended. The court decided yes: the duties are automatically suspended even though probation was granted.
raw.held: A public servant who receives a final criminal sentence of loss of public rights has their duties automatically suspended, even if the court also grants probation (a suspended sentence).

points.text: A public servant given a final criminal sentence of loss of public rights has their duties automatically suspended.

A suspended sentence only loses its effect if the probation period ends without the suspension being revoked, as the ruling reads the Civil Servant Discipline Act Article 17(2) and Criminal Code Article 76.
During the probation period the sentence has not lost its effect, so it cannot be said that the reason for suspending the duties has disappeared.
Interpretation No. 56 does not exclude applying Article 17(2) of the Civil Servant Discipline Act.

who: Public servants sentenced to loss of public rights with probation

raw.answer: The case asked whether someone who forges a document of the kind covered by Article 212 of the Criminal Code, and forges an official seal at the same time, can be punished only under Article 212. The court said no: the separate and heavier offense of forging an official seal in Article 218 cannot be ignored. It also held that its earlier interpretation (院解字第3020號, item 3) did not go against the lawmakers' intent and did not need to be changed.
raw.held: When someone forges an Article 212 document and also forges an official seal, the case cannot be punished under Article 212 alone while ignoring the heavier Article 218 offense. The earlier interpretation (院解字第3020號, item 3) stands and needs no change.

points.text: The Supreme Court had doubts about the earlier interpretation, and under an earlier council resolution the court agreed to interpret it again.
Article 212 covers forging and altering certain public and private documents, while Article 218 separately punishes forging official seals, so the seal offense cannot be left out.
The earlier interpretation does not go against the lawmakers' intent and is hard to call improper.

Forging a seal alone carries up to five years in prison, but under Article 212 alone, forging a document plus a seal would bring only up to one year, detention, or a fine of up to 300 yuan. That would be unbalanced and against the legislative intent.
For these reasons the earlier interpretation does not need to be changed.

who: People accused of forging documents together with official seals
The Supreme Court and other courts applying these provisions

raw.answer: The case arose from a dispute between a military body and the civilian courts over the same matter. The military body had decided not to prosecute, finding that the person's involvement came before the Act Punishing Rebellion took effect and did not continue afterward. The civilian courts relied on Interpretation No. 68 to say the person was still suspected of an offence under the Act. The court ruled that in martial-law areas, the military body with trial authority decides whether someone joined a rebel organization and whether the involvement continued.
raw.held: In martial-law areas, whether a person joined a rebel organization and whether that involvement continued must be decided by the military authority that has the power to try the case. Interpretation No. 68 does not apply where that authority has already found the conduct not to be an offence under the Act.

points.text: Under the latter part of Article 10 of the Act Punishing Rebellion, cases of joining a rebel organization committed in martial-law areas are tried by military authorities regardless of the person's status.
Because the military authority tries these cases, it is the one that must determine the facts of whether someone joined and whether the involvement continued.
A military finding that conduct is not an offence under the Act is hard to deny effect until it has been lawfully changed.
Interpretation No. 68 was meant for people who joined a rebel organization and did not turn themselves in or show they had truly left it.
If the competent military authority has found the conduct is not an offence under the Act, Interpretation No. 68 does not apply and raises no issue.

who: People suspected of joining a rebel organization in martial-law areas

raw.answer: The case asked whether people working for a state-owned enterprise were still public officials under criminal law before the enterprise was privatized. The court said a company-law state enterprise counts as private only once more than 50 percent of its shares are held by private shareholders after the transfer. Until the handover is actually carried out, its staff who serve under the law remain public officials for criminal law purposes.
raw.held: A state-owned company is treated as privately owned only after private shares exceed 50 percent following the transfer, even if the transfer date and the handover of profits, losses, rights and duties were already fixed. Before the handover is carried out, its employees serving under the law are still public officials under criminal law.

points.text: Fixing the transfer date and the transfer of profits, losses, rights and duties is not enough to make the enterprise private.
The enterprise is regarded as private only after the transfer leaves private shareholders with more than 50 percent.
Until the handover is actually carried out, staff serving under the law remain public officials under criminal law.

who: Employees of state-owned enterprises being privatized
State-owned enterprises organized under the company law
